discussion_comments.comment_body: Should we standardize the client names with ClientName from sdk/packages/shared/src/extensions/context.ts?

in [`728da6af`](https://github.com/cline/cline/pull/15043/commits/728da6afab) the builder takes [`client: ClientName`](https://github.com/cline/cline/pull/15043/changes#diff-326ccb878a819d0441896c2a7d6fd5079d7cf6ef7fe1a83afe7bec574cc70680R15) now, and `ClinePrivacySettingsClient` is gone. the CLI passes `cline-cli`, desktop `cline-desktop`, and the extension `cline-vscode` or `cline-jetbrains` depending on the host. desktop wasn't in the type, so I [added `"cline-desktop"`](https://github.com/cline/cline/pull/15043/changes#diff-b1dedfc4990c515060b3b09ce388c72cd1d3834ea3a557427153fe5fd65404f1R16) to `ClientName` instead of leaning on its `string & {}` escape hatch.
Since you turn around right away and write `!background`, and `background` itself is a vague (...all the checks are asynchronous) why not call this what it is: `userInitiated`?

Good call, renamed to `userInitiated` in 56021e0af so the check reads `if (userInitiated)`. One note: the initial read on mount also passes `userInitiated: true`, since it fires when the user opens the panel or switches account and the repo picker relies on that first spinner.

Valid, fixed. The hand-rolled frontmatter reader is gone; names now come from `parseSkillConfigFromMarkdown`, the same function Cline's skill loader uses (YAML rules, directory-name fallback), so the installer accepts exactly the skills the loader can load and skips the ones it would reject (which also means a SKILL.md with no instructions body is no longer treated as a skill). Covered by "reads skill names with the same YAML rules as Cline's loader" (`name: review-team # public name` and a quoted name).

I am not a huge fan of boolean fields because often enough the domain isn't actually a boolean; can we describe what this situation is, and then use strings as an enum to explain "seeded" | "written" or whatever is actually happening here?

Even with only two values, the enum is still better because it describes what "not seeded" is in a positive way, not through negation.

Right here, consider the choice someone using this file is faced with. You can call

findUsableFallbackProviderId(state): string | undefined
resolveEffectiveLastUsedProviderId(state): string | undefined

These names are terrible in terms of helping them pick the right one.

Ideal solution: Make ONE thing that everyone should call and only export that. If you want to stick some functions away in a hash to make them visible for testing, fine, but make it obvious that's what we're doing.

Not ideal but OK solution: If both of these really NEED to be public, give them names which give strong hints about which one to call when. And then give them *PERFECT* comments to remove all doubt.
